Case name: Furniture Bank, 'The Picture Isn't Real, The Reality Is' (Toronto)
Producer: Furniture Bank, a Toronto charity that redistributes donated furniture (Executive Director Dan Kershaw; images generated by an AI specialist working with the charity)
Genre: 1. Humanitarian and NGO appeals, reports and exhibitions
Country or context of the suffering depi: Canada (furniture poverty among Toronto households that lack basic furniture after moving out of a crisis)
Tool or model: Midjourney, DALL-E 2 and Stable Diffusion (named by Furniture Bank)
What the image depicts: Scenes of furniture poverty in Toronto homes, such as a person sleeping on a stained mattress, children doing homework or eating on the floor of an empty room, and a kitchen with only a sink and cupboards, many with people backlit or in silhouette (Kershaw, February 2026); the prompts were written from the stories of client families, so the generated people (type a) are presented as typical of the charity's clients.
Disclosure: statement: campaign title "The picture isn't real. The reality is." (Furniture Bank, campaign page, 2022), with the online gallery presented as the 2022 AI campaign; Dan Kershaw later argued that the campaign title served as the disclosure. Sandberg, Wasif and Hand (2025) state that donors were not told the images were AI-generated, whereas Adesina and Girling (2026) record the images as fully credited as AI-generated.
Justification given by the producer: "The choice was between AI images and nothing." (Dan Kershaw, 'Compared to What?', Substack, April 2026). The charity also said it would not photograph clients at their lowest moments, that the method respects clients' privacy and dignity and avoids what it calls poverty porn, and that AI saved up to $60,000 in production costs (the amount from Toronto Times, November 2022; the other points from Furniture Bank's campaign pages) [protection of identity; cost; absence of images]
Explicit statement that the person shown: yes: "The picture isn't real. The reality is." (Furniture Bank, campaign page, 2022; the statement concerns the images rather than named persons)
Reception and debate: The Toronto Star reported the campaign in December 2022 under a headline stressing that the fundraising image was not real. The fundraising think tank Rogare discussed the case in the introduction to its 2024 research agenda on AI and fundraising ethics and questioned the charity's claim to have resolved the problem of poverty porn, and an article in the Journal of Public Affairs Education (2025) criticised the charity for not telling donors that the images were AI-generated. Furniture Bank defended the campaign as the only affordable alternative to photographing clients in distress, argued that the campaign title was itself the disclosure, and published a self-audit of the images for racial bias in February 2026; the images remain on its website.
Policy or guideline consequence: Furniture Bank adopted a Responsible AI Manifesto in May 2023 that permits AI images of furniture poverty only where they preserve clients' dignity, rules out AI video of client experiences and states: "We specifically do not use AI-generated images as a substitute for authentic photographs" (Furniture Bank, May 2023).

Case name: Amnesty International Norway, AI illustrations of police abuses in Colombia's 2021 national strike
Producer: Amnesty International Norway (Twitter account @Amnesty_Norge)
Genre: 1. Humanitarian and NGO appeals, reports and exhibitions
Country or context of the suffering depi: Colombia (police repression of the 2021 national strike, including sexual and gender-based violence against protesters)
Tool or model: not reported in the coverage opened (the Gizmodo URL and Table 2 refer to Midjourney, unconfirmed)
What the image depicts: Illustrations posted in a Twitter thread (Gizmodo counts three), showing among other scenes a woman standing in front of flames beside a caption on police sexual violence against women and LGBTI protesters, police officers dragging away a woman wrapped in a Colombian flag, and riot police in helmets; Amnesty said it chose vivid colours, an artistic style and visible imperfections so that the images could not be mistaken for photographs, and the people depicted are fully generated (type a) but stand for the real, unnamed victims of the abuses Amnesty documented.
Truth claim: about a real event with no recordings
Disclosure: label: "illustrations produced by artificial intelligence" (small note in the lower left corner of each image, as reported by Vice and Gizmodo, May 2023)
Justification given by the producer: "Those who did show their faces are still at risk" (Amnesty International spokesperson, statement to Gizmodo, May 2023). Amnesty said that many protesters covered their faces for fear of reprisals, that many abuses happened in darkness after power cuts so that little footage exists, that it consulted partner organisations in Colombia, and that the artistic style and deliberate imperfections were meant to distinguish the images from photographs (Gizmodo and Vice, May 2023) [protection of identity; safety; absence of images]
Reception and debate: Critics included the media scholar Roland Meyer, who argued that the images devalue the work of reporters and photographers who documented the abuses, and Sam Gregory of WITNESS, who said they do more harm than good because they help authoritarian governments dismiss real footage as fake and shift the burden of proving authenticity onto journalists and human rights defenders. The Vice journalist Jason Koebler pointed to errors such as the stripes of the Colombian flag in the wrong order and distorted faces, helmets and name badges, and argued that the images weakened Amnesty's credibility as a source of verified evidence. Amnesty defended the images as a clearly labelled protective measure while stating that it had no formal policy on AI-generated images, and The Register later reported that Amnesty removed an AI-generated image of a protester in response to the criticism.
Policy or guideline consequence: WITNESS guidance on generative AI for human rights advocacy (June 2023), which links to reporting on the criticism of Amnesty's images, warns that generating visual content "takes us further away from real evidence" (WITNESS, June 2023); Amnesty itself told Gizmodo in May 2023 that it had no policy for or against AI-generated images, and no later Amnesty policy on its own use of generated images was found. Amnesty International later published the briefing Unlawful by design: Exposing the human rights costs of generative AI (28 May 2026, POL 40/0996/2026), which argues that generative AI systems built on unlawful web scraping violate human rights and should be prohibited; the briefing does not mention the 2023 Colombia images.
Evidence of the "liar's dividend": none found (Sam Gregory of WITNESS warned that such images help authoritarian governments dismiss genuine footage as fake, Gizmodo, May 2023, but no event in which real images of the strike were dismissed as AI was found)
Academic discussion: Scalvini, M. (forthcoming) 'AI-generated imagery in humanitarian communication: towards a critique of synthetic posthumanitarianism' (takes the Amnesty Colombia campaign as its point of departure); Adesina, D. and Girling, D. (2026) 'Artificial Authenticity: The Rise of Images Generated by Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Charity and Development Communications', University of East Anglia (analyses Reddit comments on a labelled 2023 Amnesty International image about conflict and violence, very probably this case, although the report does not name Colombia).

The case is the clearest test of whether a protective justification and a visible label can give a generated image evidentiary value, so it speaks to evidentiary versus appellative use and to the responsibility of the producer; the ICS article (Scalvini 2026) argues that protective justifications solve one ethical problem only by creating another, and the warning by WITNESS that such images help governments dismiss genuine footage corresponds to what Chouliaraki, Stupart and Aiello call the re-entrenchment of testimonial suspicion towards vulnerable witnesses. For alignment between the two papers: the forthcoming paper by Chouliaraki, Stupart and Aiello describes Amnesty's May 2026 briefing as a guide to AI in humanitarianism, whereas its text addresses the human rights costs of generative AI built on web scraping, which bears on epistemic extraction (Scalvini 2026) rather than on Amnesty's own image practice.

Case name: Exhibit A-i: The Refugee Account (Maurice Blackburn Lawyers with Howatson+Company)
Producer: Maurice Blackburn Lawyers (Social Justice Practice), with the creative agency Howatson+Company (credited on the site as Howatson & Company for bringing the idea and the witness statements to life through AI technology, design and creative thinking)
Genre: 1. Humanitarian and NGO appeals, reports and exhibitions
Country or context of the suffering depi: Australia's offshore immigration detention on Nauru and Manus Island (Papua New Guinea), with some statements from Christmas Island
Tool or model: Midjourney, with licensed Shutterstock images, used by the agency's designers to generate preliminary images (ABA Journal, October 2023); the project's own pages refer only to AI technology
What the image depicts: Photorealistic images generated from the written statements of people formerly held in offshore detention, depicting the conditions and events each witness described; the people depicted have no photographed referent (type a), but each image illustrates the account of a specific real witness who is kept anonymous, so the case borders on type c without the person being identifiable.
Truth claim: about a real event with no recordings
Disclosure: statement: "They are not real but the experiences they depict are." (Exhibit A-i website, 2023, following the sentence that the images were generated using AI technology); according to the digital forensics expert Hany Farid, nothing on the images themselves shows that they are AI-generated, and the captions on The Guardian's republication of the images were misleading (ABA Journal, October 2023)
Justification given by the producer: "urged us to find another way for their testimonies to be shared" (Maurice Blackburn, on the witnesses in the discontinued class action, July 2023). The project also states that camera equipment, journalists and phones were restricted or banned in the offshore detention centres, so that no visual record exists, and that all identities were kept anonymous to protect participants and their families (Exhibit A-i website, 2023). Jennifer Kanis of Maurice Blackburn told the ABA Journal that the technology made it possible to tell stories that would otherwise not have been told, that the firm wanted to preserve the statements because court records are usually destroyed after seven years, and that, since journalists and photographers were barred from the camps, the decision to use AI was itself a statement (ABA Journal, October 2023) [consent; absence of images; protection of identity]
Explicit statement that the person shown: yes: "They are not real but the experiences they depict are." (Exhibit A-i website, Maurice Blackburn, 2023)
Reception and debate: Maurice Blackburn presented the project as bearing witness to the offshore processing system and used it to call for a National Human Rights Act and a redress scheme for people injured in offshore detention; it unveiled the work at the Immigration Museum in Melbourne in April 2023 and showed it to the minister for immigration and members of Parliament (ABA Journal, October 2023). WITNESS linked to the project in June 2023 as an example of AI visuals that add missing images to written or audio testimony, while advising that such visuals be presented clearly as artistic expression rather than as a literal record. The digital forensics expert Hany Farid warned that recreating witness accounts with AI could allow real evidence to be dismissed as fake and criticised the absence of an AI label on the images: "There’s nothing on the image that shows it’s AI-generated. I think that’s a mistake" (Hany Farid, ABA Journal, October 2023). A survivor told the ABA Journal that working on the project made her relive her trauma and that she had trouble sleeping during the consultation process.
Policy or guideline consequence: Cited in WITNESS guidance on using generative AI for human rights advocacy (June 2023), which advises that visuals generated from testimony be identified as artistic expression; no resulting law or government policy found.
Evidence of the "liar's dividend": none found (Hany Farid warned in the ABA Journal, October 2023, that recreating witness accounts with AI could allow real evidence to be dismissed as fake, but no such dismissal is reported)

(2026) 'Artificial Authenticity: The Rise of Images Generated by Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Charity and Development Communications', University of East Anglia (counts 32 Maurice Blackburn images in its sample, without naming the project).

Case name: Børns Vilkår and Upland Studio, 'Stop violence against children' AI portraits of fictional children (Denmark)
Producer: Børns Vilkår (Danish children's organisation), with the design agency Upland Studio (Odder, Denmark); credits on Ads of the World: Janus Mikkel Jørnaa (head of strategy and art director) and Ditte-Marie Tehrani (copywriter)
Genre: 1. Humanitarian and NGO appeals, reports and exhibitions
Country or context of the suffering depi: Denmark (violence against children at home)
Tool or model: not reported (the agency states only that the portraits were made with AI and Photoshop, and names no AI model)
What the image depicts: Close portraits of fictional boys and girls presented as children who have experienced violence, made with AI and Photoshop, each looking directly at the viewer and given a first name and a headline that echoes what such a child might have been told (for example, that Noah could just have spoken nicely), beside a statistic on violence against children at home.
Disclosure: statement: "AI portraits of children who have been exposed to violence" (Upland Studio, campaign entry on Ads of the World, 2023); the agency's case page also states that all the children in the campaign are AI-generated, but no label on the posters or advertisements is reported in the pages opened, and the images were not viewed
Justification given by the producer: "ved hjælp af AI og photoshop, hvorfor ingen børn har lidt overlast i designprocessen" (Upland Studio, case page for Børns Vilkår, undated; in English: with the help of AI and Photoshop, which is why no children suffered harm in the design process). The same page states that AI made it possible to create closeness without subjecting real children to taking part in a process that could itself become intense, and calls the use of AI an ethical choice rather than a technical shortcut ["no children were harmed"; safety]
Explicit statement that the person shown: yes: stated on the agency's case page, which says in Danish that all the children in the campaign are AI-generated, so that no real children had to take part in material about violence (Upland Studio, case page, undated; paraphrased)
Reception and debate: No press coverage, public reaction or statement by Børns Vilkår was found in the pages that could be opened, and the World Brand Design Society page listed in the source index returned no article text. Upland Studio presents the use of AI as an ethical choice and reports that the campaign has since been analysed in the peer-reviewed journal Visual Studies (2026) with regard to ethics, visual rhetoric and representation in humanitarian communication. According to Table 2, the article by Herrie and Philipsen argues that the training data probably included real abuse material and questions the claim that no children were harmed; this could not be checked, because the publisher's page could not be opened.

Case name: Charity Right, AI-generated hungry children in Ramadan fundraising ads and A/B test
Producer: Charity Right, a UK food aid charity based in Bradford that funds school meals (case study presented by Jamal Abbas at I Wish I'd Thought of That 2023)
Genre: 1. Humanitarian and NGO appeals, reports and exhibitions
Country or context of the suffering depi: Hunger and school feeding among children in Sudan (test image), with ads also referring to children in Bangladesh and Yemen
Tool or model: not reported (Reddit users suspected Midjourney)
What the image depicts: Photorealistic images of hungry children with sad or serious expressions used in fundraising ads for school meals, including an image generated from prompts based on a real photograph of a girl in Sudan taken by the charity's own team; the children shown do not exist and stand for the charity's beneficiaries.
Disclosure: none, then statement: the ads carried no label ("The images are not labeled as AI-generated", Doc Pop, April 2023); after the campaign Charity Right disclosed that some images were AI-generated and opened a Reddit discussion (SOFII, 2025), and it published a blog post on its use of generative AI in May 2023 whose wording could not be retrieved
Justification given by the producer: "What more can we do to protect the dignity and identity of the children" (Charity Right, statement quoted in the SOFII case study, 2025); the statement goes on to cite the safety of staff who travel to document its work and the aim of spending efficiently so that more of each donation funds school meals [protection of identity; safety; cost]
Reception and debate: Reddit users noticed signs of generation, such as a child with eyes of different colours, a young girl with a moustache and a hand missing a finger, and PetaPixel and the blogger Doc Pop reported the unlabelled ads in late April 2023; commenters asked whether a charity that cannot show a real hungry child can be trusted to feed one. Charity Right told Doc Pop it would explain its use of AI in a blog post, which it published in May 2023 (not opened). The SOFII case study reports that the AI images and the real photograph raised almost identical revenue with similar click and cost rates, that the AI images received more impressions, and that the charity's Reddit discussion divided opinion between those who saw savings for beneficiaries and those who saw dishonesty; the UEA report states that the images led to public outcry on Reddit.
Policy or guideline consequence: Charity Right now uses AI images for rapid testing and top-of-funnel ads and keeps real photographs for storytelling (SOFII, 2025); no external policy found.

Case name: UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein, 'Make.Future.Happen.' AI poster exhibition for the Swiss Economic Forum (Interlaken)
Producer: UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein (a UNICEF national committee, coded as NGO rather than UN agency), through its own staff (credited on Ads of the World, including Marc Uricher, Head of Digital & Media, and Felix Freese, head of brand, who leads an in-house creative team), with twelve commissioned AI artists: Mieke Haase, Ulises (Ulises Studio), Peter Brönnimann, Denis Klook, Grit Wolany, Tanya Rey, Felix Freese, David Blum, Hekuran Avdili, Olof Lindh, The Museum of Natural Futures and Torsten Maas
Genre: 1. Humanitarian and NGO appeals, reports and exhibitions
Country or context of the suffering depi: No specific country: imagined futures of children in general (one image is set in Interlaken, and the captions of three images by Denis Klook describe an African child)
Country of the producer: Switzerland (the committee covers Switzerland and Liechtenstein)
Tool or model: Midjourney (each image on the exhibition page is credited to Midjourney together with the artist's name, and the head of brand refers to the Midjourney files)

(UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein, SEF 2023 exhibition page, image by Denis Klook; in English, an African child who will become either a soldier or professionally successful), a typified child, which brings this image close to type b.

Tool or model: Midjourney (confirmed by a WHO spokesperson in an emailed statement to NPR, October 2023)

Case name: "All Eyes on Rafah" AI-generated image spread through an Instagram story template
Producer: Disputed between two Malaysian makers of AI images (NPR, June 2024). Amirul Shah, a 21-year-old college student in Kuala Lumpur who posts on Instagram as shahv4012 and whom The Jewish Chronicle describes as a photographer, posted the Instagram story template that went viral and says he made the image with an AI generator. Zila Abka, a 39-year-old science teacher and AI art hobbyist, says she made the original image and posted it in the Facebook group Prompters Malaya, and Shah denies copying her image
Country or context of the suffering depi: Gaza, Palestinian territories (Rafah, after an Israeli strike on a tent camp for displaced people on Sunday 26 May 2024 that killed at least 45 people, as reported by Time, NBC News, Axios and Al Jazeera in May 2024)
Tool or model: Microsoft Image Creator according to Zila Abka for her version; Amirul Shah thinks he used the same service but says he cannot remember, Abka believes he extended her image with an AI tool that expands backgrounds, and NPR could not reproduce the image with Image Creator in dozens of attempts (NPR, June 2024)
What the image depicts: An aerial view of orderly rows of tents between snow-capped mountains, in which lighter tents spell out the slogan "All Eyes on Rafah" (wording as given by Quartz, May 2024), with no bodies or blood shown (Scalvini 2026, p. 23) and none of the smoke or bombed tents of the real camp (Al Jazeera, May 2024), standing for the displaced population of Rafah rather than any identifiable person (type b also applies).
Disclosure: statement (after circulation): Amirul Shah told NPR that he made the image with an AI generator, and Zila Abka that she made her version with Microsoft Image Creator (NPR, June 2024). No source opened reports an AI label or caption on the image or the template. Al Jazeera's Sanad fact-checking agency confirmed that the image was AI-generated (May 2024), and NBC News reported that none of the templates it reviewed, in a report on the wave of AI images that followed, stated that the images were made with AI, despite Meta's labelling initiative (second NBC News report, May 2024); the report does not say whether this includes the original.
Justification given by the producer: "In the world of social media, we cannot show the real picture" (Amirul Shah, to NPR, June 2024): Shah added that real pictures would be censored and users blocked, that AI images spread faster, and that he wanted justice for the Palestinians there rather than popularity, while Abka and Shah both said that AI images can capture attention [other (avoiding the removal of graphic documentary images by platforms; reach)]
Reception and debate: The template spread through Instagram's Add Yours story feature in the days after the strike and was reshared by celebrities including Bella Hadid, Dua Lipa, Nicola Coughlan and Varun Dhawan (Axios, Time, NPR, NBC News and Al Jazeera, May and June 2024). Critics called it performative activism or slacktivism and a sanitised view of the war that distracted from real images from Rafah (Axios; The Jewish Chronicle; Al Jazeera, May 2024), the photographer Daniel Etter writing that Gaza is "not a sanitized AI-generated landscape" (Instagram post quoted by Axios, May 2024) and the artist Ameera Kawash that the image "undermines Palestinian testimony and lived experience" (Al Jazeera, May 2024). In defence of the use of AI, Sarah Jackson of the Annenberg School for Communication and the social media analyst Matt Navarra argued that it allows activists to circulate a message within platform rules, which often remove graphic documentary images (Time; NBC News, May 2024), while the account shahv4012 apologised in an Instagram story to people dissatisfied with the picture and template (Time; Al Jazeera, May 2024). Pro-Israel users answered with AI images, one of which, asking where people's eyes had been on 7 October, Instagram removed on 29 May 2024 and reinstated within hours, Meta calling the removal a mistake (Axios; NBC News), while Instagram removed two of three posts showing the dead and injured after the strike and no source opened reports action against the AI image itself (NBC News; Al Jazeera, May 2024).

Case name: AI-generated poverty and suffering stock images sold on Adobe Stock and Freepik and used in NGO and aid communication ("poverty porn 2.0")
Producer: Contributors to commercial stock platforms, chiefly Adobe Stock and Freepik, which sell the images; images of the same kind were posted by NGOs, aid organisations and individual aid workers on LinkedIn and X
Genre: 1. Humanitarian and NGO appeals, reports and exhibitions
Country or context of the suffering depi: Not specific: generated people presented as poor or suffering in Africa, Asia and other parts of the Global South
Country of the producer: Various (international stock platforms and contributors; not reported for individual images)
Tool or model: not reported for the stock images; the AI images found on LinkedIn were made with Meta AI, Grok, ChatGPT/DALL-E and Midjourney (The New Humanitarian, October 2025)
What the image depicts: Typified images of poverty and need, such as a child drinking from a contaminated water source, an African girl beside an elderly man captioned as a child marriage, emaciated babies, Asian children swimming in polluted rivers and white volunteers hugging African children, sold as stills (some platforms also sell video clips).
Stated purpose: other (commercial sale as stock imagery for campaigns and fundraising)
Disclosure: label: "Gegenereerd met AI" (Dutch for Generated with AI, shown on the Adobe Stock page of the child marriage image, opened 26 October 2026); no disclosure practice by the NGOs that reuse such images is documented in the sources opened
Justification given by the producer: "We review everything that is uploaded to the current regulation" (Jose Florido, Freepik chief market development officer, interview with The Register, October 2025) [other: platform neutrality and demand]; on the NGO side, a communications officer in western Europe whose team uses Midjourney for portraits said "we cannot afford to commission photographers like the big international ones do" (quoted by Alenichev, The New Humanitarian, October 2025) [cost]
Reception and debate: An article by Arsenii Alenichev and colleagues in The Lancet Global Health (2025) gathered more than 100 AI-generated images posted on LinkedIn and X and argued, under the label "poverty porn 2.0", that they copy the conventions of older fundraising images that sensationalise poverty, and The Register reported on 20 October 2025 (the date of The Guardian's investigation) that a Freepik search for AI images of poverty returned mostly people with black and brown skin. Freepik's chief market development officer said uploads are reviewed against current regulation, that where there is demand the platform tries not to judge the potential use, and that even biased images can have acceptable uses, while Adobe described its stock service as a marketplace in which creators upload and license content under submission standards. Gareth Benest of the International Broadcasting Trust urged charities to refuse such images (The Independent, October 2025), and Children Change Colombia and Fairpicture criticised the racial stereotypes they reproduce, with Fairpicture issuing practical guidance for NGOs. Some images were deleted after press reports while others stayed on sale, and two of the Adobe Stock images linked by The New Humanitarian, which links four Adobe Stock pages, were still offered for licensing when opened on 26 October 2026.
Policy or guideline consequence: Fairpicture white paper and checklist on poverty porn in the era of generative AI, with practical guidance for NGOs (Kardol 2025); the EU-funded AIrbrush project (Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp) reports that its research evidence contributed to the removal of specific dehumanising AI-generated stock assets from an unnamed commercial marketplace (CORDIS project summary, 2026); the UEA Artificial Authenticity report (March 2026) recommends that creative teams reassess the automatic use of photorealistic AI and consider illustrative or future-oriented approaches.

Disclosure: label: Adobe Stock marks such images on its platform as "generated with AI" (Crikey, November 2023), and some titles contain the words "generative AI"; the label did not travel with downloaded copies, and the small outlets that republished the images did not mark them as AI-generated (Crikey, November 2023; The Register, November 2023).
Justification given by the producer: Adobe stated that its marketplace "requires all generative AI content to be labeled as such" (Adobe statement to Motherboard, Vice, November 2023) and that the images had been labelled on submission and at licensing [other: disclosure at the point of sale].
Reception and debate: Crikey reported in November 2023 that photorealistic generated images of the war were on sale and had been reused unlabelled, and an RMIT researcher it interviewed warned that they could mislead audiences, while Crikey itself raised the labour implications of using them instead of photographers on the ground; Vice, Business Insider, The Register, The Decoder and Cyber Daily followed. A check by the blogger Nick Heer found that most reuses were on minor blogs rather than established newsrooms, but that a small Georgia news site, Now Habersham, had used a generated image of a Ukrainian residential building destroyed by a bomb; its publisher said the staff had "overlooked the notation that it was A.I.-generated" (Pixel Envy, November 2023) and replaced it with a real photograph. The Washington Post, as summarised by InsideHook and the AI Incident Database, found more than 3,000 images labelled as AI-generated among results for the search term Gaza and more than 15,000 for the search term Ukraine war, some of them unlabelled, but no sign that any had gone viral; it also noted that Getty Images had banned AI-generated images while Shutterstock hosted labelled AI images related to Gaza. The Forward found that iStock, owned by Getty Images, also offered rendered images of a burning Jerusalem and that iStock appeared to be removing some of the more incendiary items after its inquiry.
Policy or guideline consequence: Adobe Stock announced new rules in November 2023: contributors may no longer submit generative AI content with "titles that imply that it is depicting an actual newsworthy event" (Adobe blog, November 2023), editorial uses may not mislead or deceive, labelling was to be made clearer before licensing, and Content Credentials were to be attached to downloaded generative AI assets. The same post acknowledged community concern that generated war-like images were being used on social media to describe the Israel-Hamas war misleadingly. The AI Incident Database lists the case as Incident 613, whose title states that AI images on Adobe Stock misrepresent real-world events.

Producer: The X user @stellarman22, identified by Open (citing Provereno.media) as the maker of the composite, who described it as a quick fake; LeBigData attributes the AI edit to 4chan users, where the composite was posted as the supposed original; it was then reshared on X, Facebook and Russian-language Telegram channels and presented as the original by an Al Jazeera Arabic programme

Tool or model: not reported

Case name: Republican National Committee 'Beat Biden' advertisement built with AI imagery
Producer: Republican National Committee (RNC), published on its YouTube channel on the day Joe Biden announced his re-election campaign; the RNC did not name the image generator
Country or context of the suffering depi: United States (the imagined scenes include a Chinese invasion of Taiwan)
Tool or model: not reported (the RNC named no generator; Sam Gregory of WITNESS guessed Midjourney, and Gizmodo, citing The Verge, called Stable Diffusion very possible)

Country or context of the suffering depi: France and the European Union (migration to Europe)
Tool or model: not reported

Tool or model: Arcana (Arcana Labs)

Case name: Lega and Matteo Salvini AI-generated images of crimes attributed to migrants
Producer: Lega, through the official Lega and Matteo Salvini pages on Facebook, Instagram and X
Country or context of the suffering depi: Italy
Tool or model: not reported

Case name: Facebook engagement-bait pages posting AI images of amputees, poor and starving children and disabled veterans
Producer: Networks of spam and scam Facebook pages documented by Renée DiResta (Stanford Internet Observatory) and Josh A. Goldstein (Georgetown CSET) in a study of 120 pages, and by 404 Media and Futurism: for example the pages Anita Kumari (emaciated people and starving children) and Dream Home (images of poor Black children), and Summer Vibes (an AI-generated disabled woman veteran in a wheelchair). 404 Media and Gizmodo reported that many operators are based in India, Vietnam, the Philippines, Pakistan, Thailand and Indonesia and earn money through Facebook's creator bonus programme.
Country or context of the suffering depi: not specific (generic images of poverty, disability and military injury, many aimed at US audiences)
Country of the producer: India, Vietnam, the Philippines and other South and Southeast Asian countries (as reported); some page operators in Armenia, the United States and Georgia (DiResta and Goldstein)
Tool or model: not reported for specific pages; Gizmodo and Futurism report that such spammers use Microsoft's AI image creator
What the image depicts: Fully generated people presented as real persons asking for sympathy: elderly people, amputees and infants captioned with complaints that no one had blessed them, poor or starving children, children posing with handmade wooden sculptures, and a young woman in army fatigues in a wheelchair presented as a disabled veteran.
Disclosure: none reported: DiResta and Goldstein found few labelled images on the pages they studied, and the caption of the veteran image, "Please don't swip [sic] up without giving some love" (Summer Vibes page, quoted by Futurism, June 2024), contains no disclosure.
Justification given by the producer: none found; a Hindi-language YouTube tutorial reported by 404 Media presents such pages as a way to earn Facebook's performance bonus and remarks: "The Indian audience is very emotional" (tutorial quoted by 404 Media, August 2024) [other: monetisation].
Reception and debate: DiResta and Goldstein's preprint found that such pages received hundreds of millions of engagements and exposures, that one post had 40 million views, and that many commenters did not recognise the images as synthetic; it recommended platform labelling and watermarking. Jason Koebler of 404 Media traced the trade to creators paid by Facebook's bonus programme, and Futurism reported tutorials recommending prompts such as "poor people thin body" (tutorial quoted by Futurism, August 2024); Futurism also described thousands of sincere comments thanking the generated veteran for her service. Meta stated, as reported by Gizmodo, that it encourages creators to use AI tools to produce high-quality content, and no removal of the pages is reported in these sources.
Policy or guideline consequence: none found specific to these pages; DiResta and Goldstein note Meta's announced plan to label detectable AI-generated images, which they found little applied in practice.

Case name: AI-enhanced collage of eight Iranian women political prisoners shared with execution claim (Trump, White House, State Department)
Producer: Collage maker not identified (neither Tech Policy Press nor Maldita attributes it). The Lawfare Project, a legal advocacy organisation based in New York, published the image of the eight women on Facebook and Instagram on 19 March 2026 with the claim that all had been sentenced to death (Maldita, April 2026); the pro-Israel activist Eyal Yakoby posted it on X on 20 April 2026 with a claim that Iran was preparing to hang the eight women, and President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of that post on Truth Social on 21 April 2026 (Lead Stories, April 2026); amplified by the @WhiteHouse account on X and republished in translation by the State Department's Persian-language Instagram account @usabehfarsi.
Producer type: other (unidentified creator, circulated by an advocacy organisation and an activist and amplified by the US government)
Country or context of the suffering depi: Iran (political prisoners arrested after the January 2026 protests)
Tool or model: not reported
What the image depicts: A grid of the faces of eight real Iranian women detained after the January 2026 protests (including Bita Hemmati, Mahboubeh Shabani and Diana Taherabadi), whose photographs had been retouched with stylised black backgrounds, beauty filtering and smoothing; in reply, the Iranian Embassy in South Africa posted a grid of eight fully AI-generated women in hijab (type a).
Disclosure: none reported: Tech Policy Press describes no label or caption indicating that the photographs had been altered (Tech Policy Press, April 2026).
Justification given by the producer: none found
Reception and debate: Online users and Iranian diplomatic accounts, including the embassy in South Africa and the consulate in Hyderabad, claimed that the women were AI-generated (Maldita; WION, April 2026), and Lead Stories rated that claim false after Iran Human Rights (Oslo) confirmed that the women are real prisoners, of whom only one, Bita Hemmati, has a confirmed death sentence. Iran's judiciary called the execution claim false, and the Iranian Embassy in South Africa mocked the confusion with a grid of fully generated women captioned as eight other girls to be executed. Mahsa Alimardani of WITNESS argued in Tech Policy Press that the visible AI retouching made documented human rights cases look fabricated, which allowed the Iranian state to dismiss real abuses: "The real women in real prisons disappear into the noise" (Mahsa Alimardani, Tech Policy Press, April 2026).
Policy or guideline consequence: none found specific to the case; Tech Policy Press discusses it alongside the Meta Oversight Board's recommendations on labelling deceptive AI content during conflicts and X's announcement in March 2026 that creators posting unlabelled AI videos of armed conflict would be suspended from revenue sharing. Recorded as Incident 1468 in the AI Incident Database.
Evidence of the "liar's dividend": Yes: users claimed that the real women were AI-generated, a claim Lead Stories rated false (Lead Stories, April 2026), and the Iranian embassy in South Africa and consulate in Hyderabad accused Trump of having generated the image of the eight women with AI (Maldita, April 2026; WION, April 2026); Tech Policy Press argues that the confusion helped the Iranian state deny the underlying cases, citing the judiciary's description of the post as fake news and the embassy's mocking grid of generated women (Tech Policy Press, April 2026).

Case name: Turkey and Syria earthquake: Midjourney firefighter image reused in cryptocurrency donation appeal
Producer: Image made by Panagiotis Kotridis, a retired major general of the Hellenic Fire Service and former regional fire service commander in the Aegean, as a tribute to Greek rescuers working in Turkey (Proto Thema, February 2023); reused by an unnamed Twitter account that posted the same donation appeal, with two cryptocurrency wallet addresses, eight times in 12 hours (BBC, February 2023).
Country or context of the suffering depi: Turkey and Syria (earthquakes of February 2023)
Country of the producer: Greece (image creator); country of the appeal account not reported
Tool or model: Midjourney and Photoshop (creator's account reported by Proto Thema; the BBC cited the Greek newspaper OEMA for Midjourney and obtained similar images from the same tool)
What the image depicts: A firefighter in rescue gear holding a small child among collapsed buildings, described by its creator as a Greek rescuer with a child freed from the rubble; one of the firefighter's hands has six fingers, and the creator combined Midjourney output with Photoshop editing.
Disclosure: none: the donation appeal gave no indication that the image was generated; the creator's own post had presented it as a composition rather than a photograph (Proto Thema, February 2023).
Justification given by the producer: The account holder denied running a scam and told the BBC: "My aim is to be able to help people affected by the earthquake" (account holder, statement to the BBC quoted by Digital Camera World, February 2023), but sent no receipts or proof of identity [other: fundraising for victims]. The original creator made the image to honour colleagues engaged in rescue work (Proto Thema, February 2023) [other: tribute to rescuers].

Reception and debate: Twitter users identified the image as generated from the extra finger, Greek media reported that a retired fire officer had made it with Midjourney, and the BBC's Blue Room team produced near-identical images from a similar prompt. The BBC found that one wallet address had appeared in scam and spam tweets in 2018 and the other on the Russian network VK, and reported the account holder's denial; Popular Science, Digital Camera World and PetaPixel presented the case as a warning about AI-generated images in disaster charity fraud. The BBC also reported that Twitter suspended a separate appeal account and that PayPal closed a fraudulent account, while TikTok said it was working to stop scammers exploiting the earthquakes.

Case name: AI-generated portraits and invented biographies of Holocaust victims on monetised Facebook pages
Producer: Anonymous administrators of Facebook pages including 90's History, Timeless Tales, Historical Snapshots, Ok 30 and Код 4 5 0; Meta had given 90's History and Historical Snapshots verified status
Country or context of the suffering depi: Nazi-occupied Poland (mainly Auschwitz-Birkenau); the victims named came from the Netherlands, France, Germany and Poland
Country of the producer: Not established; investigators placed administrators in Myanmar, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Nigeria, Iran and Australia, and some pages named United States companies that could not be found in company registries
Tool or model: not reported
What the image depicts: Photorealistic portraits presented as photographs of named Holocaust victims, for example a polished portrait of the Dutch deportee Helena Waterman-de Jong that replaced her archival photograph, an invented birthday scene for the murdered French child Léon Gorfinkel, and a girl on a tricycle captioned as a 13-year-old Berliner killed at Auschwitz (Yad Vashem records a Hannelore Kaufmann from western Germany who died at Sobibor); some portraits were wholly invented (type a) and some were real archival photographs of victims altered with AI (type d).
Disclosure: none: the pages captioned the images as portraits of victims with no AI label; the Auschwitz Memorial stated: "These are not real photos of the victims" (Auschwitz Memorial, statement quoted by Jewish News, May 2025)
Justification given by the producer: none found
Reception and debate: The Auschwitz Memorial condemned the posts in May 2025 as disrespectful to the memory of those murdered at Auschwitz, and its deputy spokesperson Pawel Sawicki said that "producing artificial information, last names, is falsifying history" (Pawel Sawicki, quoted by AFP in The Peninsula, May 2025), warning that invented victims could help those who claim the Holocaust was made up; the Holocaust Educational Trust said this use of generative AI threatens Holocaust education. Investigations by the fact-checker Provereno (reported by OCCRP and republished by EDMO), AFP and the BBC traced the pages to administrators in several countries who post at high volume, in the investigators' assessment to earn engagement payments, with names taken from Yad Vashem and photographs taken from the Memorial's own posts. Meta told the Memorial in May 2025 that the content did not breach its policies and would stay online; after the BBC inquiry in August 2025 it removed some pages and accounts for impersonation or inauthentic behaviour.
Policy or guideline consequence: No platform rule change found. Meta's position, as reported, was that "the fabricated Holocaust photos themselves do not breach its policies" (Jewish News, reporting Meta's statement to the BBC, August 2025), although it removed several pages for breaching its authenticity rules (NOS, August 2025). The BBC findings were cited by the Bildungsstätte Anne Frank in its January 2026 demand that platforms enforce AI labelling and exclude such accounts from monetisation programmes.
Evidence of the "liar's dividend": none found (the Auschwitz Memorial warned that invented victims could be used to claim the whole history was made up, but no instance of a real image being dismissed as AI is reported)
Academic discussion: none found in the sources opened (academic databases not yet searched for this case)

Producer: Not identified: a Facebook page that claims to publish historical photographs (unnamed in the fact-check) and an X account named Petros Van Ripper (linked by Eurovision News Spotlight and named by SRF); the American actor Michael Rapaport amplified the image and later deleted his post

Tool or model: not reported

Case name: AI-generated scenes of Nazi camps and their liberation contested by German memorial sites (open letter of January 2026)
Producer: Anonymous Facebook and TikTok pages named in reporting, including Old is Gold, 90 S History, Old Life Revisited, Whispers of History, History Timelines, History Icon, Legacy Library, Deutsche Nostalgie and Die Kriegschronik; the contesting party was a coalition of German memorial sites coordinated by the Netzwerk Digital History und Memory (90's History also appears in the case of AI portraits of named Holocaust victims)
Country or context of the suffering depi: Germany (Nazi concentration camps, including Hadamar, Buchenwald, Bergen-Belsen, Dachau, Flossenbürg and Sandbostel) and occupied Poland (Auschwitz)
Country of the producer: Not established; German memorial staff said the creators are partly based in Asia (Nordkurier, April 2026)
Tool or model: not reported (one Bergen-Belsen image carried a Grok label, according to Amateur Photographer)
What the image depicts: Photorealistic scenes presented as historical photographs, such as prisoners reunited with their liberators, crying children behind barbed wire, an American soldier carrying two children in striped camp clothing out of Buchenwald, an emaciated man standing in the snow at Flossenbürg, and the supposed liberation of the Hadamar killing centre showing barracks that never existed; a recoloured photograph of the murdered Auschwitz prisoner Czesława Kwoka with her facial injuries removed was also cited (type d); reporting refers to such content on Facebook, TikTok and YouTube (the letter itself names no platform), and all the examples described are still images.
Disclosure: none: the posts circulated without AI labels; the memorials' first demand on labelling reads "Label AI-generated content, without exception" (open letter, English version, KZ-Gedenkstätte Dachau, January 2026)
Justification given by the producer: none found
Reception and debate: On 13 January 2026 more than 30 German memorial sites, archives and museums (70 entries including later co-signatories, according to a signatory list published by the Gedenkstättenforum) published an open letter stating that "AI-generated content distorts history by trivializing and kitschification" (open letter, quoted by Reuters via CP24, January 2026), and that the posts exploit the victims for profit. Arne Jost of the Hadamar memorial said that "Holocaust und NS-Verbrechen klicken sich eben gut" (hessenschau, January 2026), and memorial historians warned that the fakes devalue research and lead users to doubt authentic documents. The Culture Minister Wolfram Weimer supported the letter, stating that "Das große Leid der Opfer des Holocaust darf nicht verfälscht und verzerrt werden" (Jüdische Allgemeine, January 2026). Meta said it had removed several reported accounts for inauthentic behaviour but that reliable detection of AI content is not yet technically possible, and TikTok said it was testing watermarks and metadata labelling and would exclude the accounts from monetisation.
Policy or guideline consequence: The open letter asks platforms to act proactively against AI content that distorts history, to make it reportable as misinformation, to exclude such accounts from all monetisation programmes, to label all AI-generated content and to work with memorial sites on detection. Weimer asked the European Commission to hold platforms to account under the Digital Services Act, including labelling, removal where necessary and an end to monetisation (Jüdische Allgemeine, January 2026). TikTok told memorial staff it would exclude the accounts from monetisation and introduce automated verification (AFP via Malay Mail, January 2026).
Evidence of the "liar's dividend": Claimed by the memorials without a documented instance: the open letter states that users "zunehmend auch authentische historische Dokumente anzweifeln" (epd via Sonntagsblatt, January 2026), and Uwe Neumärker of the Foundation for the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe warned of coming problems with historical photographs in general (taz, January 2026).
Academic discussion: none found (the case is discussed in an interview with Andrew Hoskins, chair in AI, Memory and War at the University of Edinburgh, in Next, February 2026, which is journalism rather than a scholarly reference)

Case name: Welcome to Chechnya: AI face doubles for LGBTQ people fleeing persecution
Producer: David France (director); visual effects supervisor Ryan Laney, who developed the face-replacement process; broadcast by HBO
Country or context of the suffering depi: Russia (Chechnya)
Tool or model: custom face-replacement process developed by Ryan Laney (called Censor Veil in The Batch), combining an autoencoder with conventional visual effects
What the image depicts: Interview and observational footage of gay men and women fleeing persecution in Chechnya, in which the faces of 23 subjects (and in many cases their voices) were replaced with the faces of volunteers, mostly LGBTQ activists in New York, while the subjects' own expressions were kept; the disguise is removed for Maxim Lapunov, called Grisha in the film, when he speaks publicly under his own name.

Producer: Islam Nour, a designer based in China with more than 50,000 followers across social media (SBS), who runs the Instagram account in.visualart, whose profile states that its images are made with Photoshop, Illustrator and AI tools (An-Nahar); the unlabelled copies were spread by accounts that the fact-checks do not name
Country or context of the suffering depi: Gaza, Palestinian territories (the strikes that followed the resumption of the war on 18 March 2025, as cited by An-Nahar)
Country of the producer: China (where the designer is based, according to SBS, October 2024)
Tool or model: not reported (the maker refers to AI tools and Photoshop without naming a model)
What the image depicts: A weeping woman sitting near rubble and holding a skeletal body, presented in circulation as a mother in Gaza embracing the remains of her son after searching for him for a year and a half (other images by the same maker show a dog lunging at an elderly woman during a military operation and the release of the director of al-Shifa hospital).

Producer: Creator not identified. Some Arabic-language news sites, including alwatanvoice.com, published the image as an illustrative example (Open, 24 May 2025); accounts sharing the story in solidarity with Gaza then spread it as a photograph of the doctor, among them the X account @AbujomaaGaza in a two-image collage with about 26,000 likes and 13,000 reposts (Sheri Oz, citing the researcher Tal Hagin, 25 May 2025), and the journalist Joan Roura posted the story with two AI-generated photos on 27 May 2025 (Open, 29 May 2025).
Producer type: other (unidentified creator; spread by solidarity accounts on X and Facebook and by Arabic-language news sites)
Country or context of the suffering depi: Gaza, Palestinian territories (Israeli strike in May 2025 that killed nine of the ten children of Alaa al-Najjar, a doctor at the Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, as reported by the BBC and cited by Open)
Tool or model: not reported
What the image depicts: A woman in a spotless white hospital coat, her face not shown and her hands without any mark of the bombing, crying before the bodies of children in a hospital, presented as Dr Alaa al-Najjar mourning her children (Open, May 2025) (type b also applies, since the news sites that first used it presented it as an illustration rather than a portrait).
Disclosure: caption (at first publication only): some Arabic-language news sites presented the image as an illustrative example ("esempio illustrativo", Open's Italian rendering of the label, 24 May 2025); the collage on X and the retellings on Facebook carried no label, and the image was taken as a photograph of the doctor (Open, May 2025; Sheri Oz, May 2025).
Justification given by the producer: none found
Reception and debate: Open's fact-checker David Puente showed that a post shared on social media had presented an older photograph of another family as the doctor with one of her children, and found that the second image, showing a woman unharmed and spotless in a hospital coat, appeared to have been generated with AI (Open, 24 May 2025). The researcher Tal Hagin said that the AI image had probably served outlets as an illustrative cover and was then taken as real by people who rushed to find imagery without checking it, while stating that he saw nothing to suggest that the nine children had not been killed (Sheri Oz, May 2025). Case name: AI-generated image of a small boy buried under rubble shared as a victim of the January 2025 Tibet earthquake (China)
Producer: An unnamed self-media creator posted the original AI video of the scene on 18 November 2024 with a statement that it was AI-generated and later deleted it (CCTV; Wen Wei Po); after the Dingri earthquake of 7 January 2025 a netizen from Qinghai reposted the image with captions linking it to the earthquake, and other self-media accounts spread it, some soliciting donations (OECD AI Incidents Monitor).
Country or context of the suffering depi: China (Tibet, Dingri earthquake of 7 January 2025)
Tool or model: not reported
What the image depicts: A small boy lies trapped under the rubble of a collapsed building, one of his hands showing six fingers.
Disclosure: label (original only): the creator's video of 18 November 2024 stated that it was AI-generated (Wen Wei Po; CCTV), but the reposts after the earthquake carried no such statement; an expert cited by CCTV observed that many platforms add a label of suspected AI generation only about an hour after AI-generated images and videos are posted (CCTV, January 2025).
Justification given by the producer: none found

Producer: World Jewish Congress (its executive director of communications strategy, Cory Weiss, spoke for the organisation)
Country or context of the suffering depi: the Netherlands and Germany (the Holocaust: Anne Frank, who hid in Amsterdam and died in Bergen-Belsen)
Tool or model: not reported
What the image depicts: A 23-second reel in which a girl who appears to be Anne Frank, seated at a desk, smiles and then lowers her eyes to write in a notebook, made by animating photographs that the producer says are in the public domain; the only authentic film of Anne Frank is a different recording.

Case name: Hassan al-Abbasi, AI-generated image of the presumed fate of the six children of the disappeared Syrian doctor Rania al-Abbasi, recirculated as a still from an execution video

Country or context of the suffering depi: Syria (the detention in Damascus in March 2013 of Rania al-Abbasi, her six children and her secretary, after the arrest of her husband, under the former government)
Tool or model: not reported (the maker says only that he used AI)
What the image depicts: A blurred person in military uniform leading away children with indistinct features, made as an expressive image of what may have happened to Rania al-Abbasi's children (the children are real, named victims, although their faces are not recognisable).
Truth claim: about a real event with no recordings
Disclosure: statement (after circulation): Hassan al-Abbasi publicly stated that he was the first to post the image and that he had made it with AI (An-Nahar, June 2026); the sources do not say whether his original post or the copies that spread carried a label, and the copies were shared as stills from a video of the children's execution

Notes for the paper: A bereaved brother made an expressive AI image of what may have happened to his sister's disappeared children, and Facebook accounts turned it into a still from an execution video, so that the same picture served as appeal for the family and as evidence for strangers (evidentiary versus appellative use). What the image depicts: Javier Valdez, the Sinaloa journalist murdered in 2017, shown in his Panama hat speaking to camera for one minute and 39 seconds, asking President López Obrador and the state governors to stop violence against journalists and to solve his murder and those of other journalists (deepfake built from sourced footage of Valdez, with a voice blended from recordings of three actors).
Disclosure: statement: the campaign communiqué attributed the video to Propuesta Cívica and Griselda Triana, and Mexican media reported it as a deepfake recreation (Vanguardia and El Universal, 29 October 2020); whether the video carried an on-screen label was not established.

(Andrey Tyukavkin, interviewed by D&AD, 2021); Propuesta Cívica presented the campaign as a way for society to value the press ("la sociedad puede empezar a valorar a la prensa", Sara Mendiola, executive director of Propuesta Cívica, quoted by El Universal, October 2020) [consent; other (a murdered journalist's demand for justice restated through his likeness)]
Reception and debate: Mexican media reported the video widely in October 2020 under headlines built on its line that the journalist could not be killed twice, and no criticism of the video itself was found in the sources opened. The campaign won the Grand Prix for Good at Cannes Lions in 2021 and three D&AD Pencils, and the agency reported 349 million organic impressions. The agency also reported that Propuesta Cívica credited the video with helping to move Valdez's criminal case forward, a claim not independently confirmed.
Policy or guideline consequence: none found (the agency's claim that the campaign helped advance the prosecution of Valdez's killers was not independently confirmed)
Evidence of the "liar's dividend": none found (El Universal's explainer on the video discussed the liar's dividend only in general terms)

Case name: Listen To Our Voices (also reported as Listen to My Voice): D-ID animations of five Israeli women murdered by their partners warning other women (Shiran Melamdovsky Somech with DIBOOR and D-ID)
Producer: Initiated by the social technology entrepreneur Shiran Melamdovsky Somech and made with the Israeli advertising agency DIBOOR on the technology of the AI company D-ID, in collaboration with the Local Government Center, with Facebook Israel, Natural Intelligence, Outbrain and Cognate as partners; Reuters described it as an Israeli public education campaign
Producer type: other (social entrepreneur with an advertising agency and an AI company)
Country or context of the suffering depi: Israel (women killed by their partners; rise in domestic violence during the pandemic)
Tool or model: D-ID (named by the producers and in Reuters reporting): deep learning animation of photographs taken before the women died, with voices and gestures from professional actresses
What the image depicts: Animated photographs of five women murdered by their partners, among them Michal Sela, stabbed by her husband in 2019 in front of their infant daughter, each saying that she was murdered, describing how the abuse began and urging women in similar relationships to tell someone close and a domestic violence specialist.
Disclosure: statement: the campaign was announced as AI animation by D-ID with actresses' voices (NoCamels and Reuters, November 2021), and in each video the woman states that she was murdered; whether the videos carry an AI label was not established.
Justification given by the producer: Sela's sister Lili Ben Ami called the campaign a "vaccine against violence, which we are attacking from all angles" (Reuters, republished by Algemeiner, November 2021); the producers tied it to the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women and to the rise in domestic violence during the pandemic, aiming to warn women of the danger of leaving an abusive partner [consent; other (prevention: warning women at risk in the victims' own name)]
Reception and debate: Relatives described the videos as a gift and a means of prevention, Sagit Ozeri's father saying "It was a present to have her for another minute." (NoCamels, November 2021). The campaign was reported in Israel and abroad, including Brazilian technology press, which linked D-ID to the MyHeritage feature that animates photographs of dead relatives. A study of viewer comments found mostly support because of the cause, alongside misunderstandings of the technology caused by its realism and a felt conflict between the dead women's autonomy and the prosocial use of their likeness (Lowenstein, Steinfeld and Rosenberg, 2025). No withdrawal was found.
Policy or guideline consequence: Cited as a case study under the Partnership on AI's Synthetic Media Framework: D-ID's case submission (published by PAI in 2024) states that the Framework guided it on "how to inform viewers that the subjects were created using generative AI" and on consent for the likeness of deceased people, and that D-ID re-evaluated its internal processes as a result; no law or binding rule was found.
Academic discussion: Lowenstein, H., Steinfeld, N. and Rosenberg, H. (2025) 'The Ethical Implications of Prosocial Synthetic Resuscitation: Analysing User Comments to a Deepfake Campaign Addressing Intimate Partner Violence', Journal of Creative Communications, 20(1), pp. 23 to 40 (doi 10.1177/09732586241276984); Leibowicz, C. The campaign is the earliest documented case in this genre of AI-animated femicide victims speaking in the first person to prevent further killings, and its families helped write and reviewed the scripts, which makes it a reference point for participation as remedy, and an industry framework (Partnership on AI) has used it to define consent for the likeness of the dead. Producer: The Joshua Ribera Foundation, the knife crime charity founded by his mother Alison Cope, with McCann London (in-house production Craft London; directors Brightnight, the alias of the McCann creatives Elliot Lee and Rory Peyton-Jones, who devised the campaign), released through SBTV; voice built by Native Studios; lyrics ghost-written by ShadowCV and T-Roadz with Alison Cope
Country or context of the suffering depi: United Kingdom (fatal stabbing in Selly Oak, Birmingham, in 2013, and knife crime among young people)
Tool or model: not reported (deepfake technology for the face, method not described; the voice was rebuilt by Native Studios from a base recording manipulated with samples, other voices, autotune and formant shifting, and checked with his former crew)
What the image depicts: Joshua Ribera, the Birmingham grime MC known as Depzman who was stabbed to death in 2013, shown as he looked when he died and rapping a new song about his childhood, his career and the night he was killed (deepfake face with a reconstructed voice).
Disclosure: statement: the launch materials and trade coverage presented the film as made with deepfake technology (shots, 31 October 2022; Marketing Beat, October 2022); whether the video itself carries an on-screen label was not established.
Justification given by the producer: "The goal was to ultimately save lives." (Alison Cope, interviewed by MediaCat, December 2022); "It was never about bringing Josh back" (Alison Cope, Birmingham Eastside); she described the film as a tool for her talks in schools, youth centres and prisons and for her call to make youth violence education compulsory [consent; other (prevention of knife crime through the victim's own story)]
Reception and debate: Reported reach varies between sources, from 150,000 views within days (Birmingham Eastside) to one million within hours according to McCann's chief creative officer (MediaCat) and more than four million according to Marketing Beat, which also reported shares by the artists Jaykae, JME and Skepta and plans to show the film in 65 UK prisons. Academic discussion: none found in the sources opened (academic databases not yet searched for this case)

Tool or model: not reported (the company that built the AI wished to remain anonymous, according to NoCamels)

Justification given by the producer: The children "cannot speak or make their voices heard on their own" (Shiran Melamdovsky Somech, NoCamels, November 2023); she added that the campaign lets the hostages speak for themselves and builds more empathy than other advocacy, and that she first obtained the consent of the Shoham family [consent; other (giving voice to hostages who cannot speak; empathy)]

NoCamels reports coverage in Israel and abroad, including by i24 News and the Times of India, and a German version with further translations planned. Notes for the paper: Be Their Voice gives AI-generated speech to living child hostages, with the consent of their family, and its initiator had earlier run a similar campaign for Israeli victims of domestic abuse. It speaks to participation as remedy, because family consent and input stand in for the children's own voice, and to the responsibility of the producer, since the words attributed to the children were delivered by voice actors in their names, which bears on what Scalvini (2026) calls delanguaging. The case was found under the lead on hostages for genre 4 and is coded as genre 7 because it gives AI voices to victims in an advocacy campaign. Participation: Melamdovsky Somech first contacted the Shoham family for consent and to learn about the children's personalities, and NoCamels reports that the families played a key role and that families of other hostages asked for videos of their own relatives (NoCamels, November 2023). Case name: Fichas vivas de búsqueda: AI-animated photographs and synthetic voices of disappeared people demanding justice (Colectivo Luz de Esperanza, Jalisco, with Alas de Libertad)
Producer: Colectivo Luz de Esperanza (Desaparecidos Jalisco), a collective of relatives of disappeared people founded in 2021, with the volunteer network Alas de Libertad; the 2026 relaunch names Justicia Unida and Find Hope (technology, programmes and design) as partners
Country or context of the suffering depi: Mexico (disappearances in Jalisco; more than 100,000 people disappeared nationally according to The Daily Beast in 2024, and more than 130,000 according to Grupo Animal in 2026)
Tool or model: not reported (generative AI animation of each person's photograph and AI voice generation; no product is named)
What the image depicts: Photographs of people who disappeared in Jalisco, among them Héctor Daniel Flores, taken from his home in Guadalajara in May 2021 at the age of 19, animated to speak in the first person with a synthetic voice about how they disappeared and to call on the authorities to investigate.
Disclosure: statement: the collective presents the format publicly as AI-generated search posters, and reports describe the voices and likenesses as AI-made (The Daily Beast, April 2024; Grupo Animal, May 2026); whether each video carries an on-screen label was not established.
Justification given by the producer: Luz de Esperanza and Alas de Libertad announced videos with "nuestras y nuestros familiares ausentes, contando los hechos de su desaparición" (Alas de Libertad and Luz de Esperanza, joint statement quoted by Excélsior, December 2023) as part of a campaign for the dissemination of cases, justice and the return alive of all the disappeared; Luz de Esperanza says the format creates more empathy than traditional search posters, counters the stigma that blames the disappeared for their fate and puts faces to the statistics [consent; other (visibility of the disappeared and a demand for justice and for their return alive)]
Reception and debate: Mexican and US media reported the videos from December 2023 (Excélsior, The Daily Beast), and in 2026 the collective relaunched the format with a video aimed at visitors to the football World Cup co-hosted by Mexico, contrasting public spending on the tournament with the much smaller funds allocated to searches. Relatives describe the videos as painful, Héctor Flores saying "Son difíciles de ver para nosotros." (Grupo Animal, May 2026), and the collective warns that criminals could use AI to extort families; in May 2025 Mexico's National Search Commission warned that criminal groups fabricate audio, photographs and videos of disappeared people from material posted by search families and send them to relatives as false proof of life (UnoTV, May 2025). University researchers present the project as a disruptive appropriation of commercial AI while noting dependence on outside technical partners, privacy and surveillance risks and digital divides. No criticism of the collective was found.

The case is the clearest bottom-up use in the genre: relatives write and approve the words that the generated likeness speaks, which makes it the strongest test of participation as remedy and reverses what the ICS article (Scalvini 2026) calls delanguaging, since those affected keep control of situated meaning-making. Case name: The Shotline: AI-recreated voices of people killed by guns calling members of Congress (Change the Ref and March For Our Lives, with MullenLowe)
Producer: Change the Ref (founded by Manuel and Patricia Oliver, parents of Joaquin Oliver) and March For Our Lives, with the agency MullenLowe (Boston) and the production company Edisen; audio supplied by the victims' families
Country or context of the suffering depi: United States (gun deaths in Parkland, Florida; Uvalde, Texas; and other places)
Tool or model: ElevenLabs (named by Northeastern Global News, March 2024); the producers' own pages refer only to AI and deep machine learning applied to audio supplied by families
What the image depicts: Cloned voices of named people killed by guns, among them Joaquin Oliver (17, Parkland), Uziyah Garcia (10, Uvalde), Ethan Song (15), Jaycee Webster (20), Akilah Dasilva (23) and Michael Baughan, each telling in the first person how they died and asking members of Congress to change gun laws, sent as automated calls and voicemails.
Disclosure: statement: "Using ai technology, we re-created the voices of those shot and killed by guns" (The Shotline website, theshotline.org); according to the launch press release, the call scripts also tell lawmakers that AI was used, Joaquin Oliver's script stating that his parents used AI to recreate his voice (March For Our Lives, 14 February 2024).
Justification given by the producer: "Some might judge me because I'm using artificial intelligence" (Manuel Oliver, launch press release, March For Our Lives, 14 February 2024), who argued that the politicians who fail to act are the ones to be judged; the organisers cite gun deaths as the leading cause of death among US children and lawmakers who offer sympathy without acting, and present the calls as letting the victims speak to those who did not act [consent; other (absence of the victims' own voices: the dead cannot speak for themselves)]
Reception and debate: Trade and news coverage reported the launch at a rally outside the US Capitol on the sixth anniversary of the Parkland shooting, and the campaign was said to have sent more than 119,000 calls by March 2024 and more than 160,000 by September 2024. Families also played the voices to legislators in the corridors of Congress, where some were receptive, and one mother said that the door was shut in her face when she went to see the representative Andy Ogles (WSMV, February 2024); the Uvalde father Brett Cross said the voices let families reach politicians who "have been hearing us but not listening to us" (ABC13, February 2024). A Northeastern University voice technology researcher, Rupal Patel, defended the campaign as a creative use made acceptable by parental consent and to be judged case by case, whereas the criminologist James Alan Fox found the synthetic voice "contrived" and distracting and urged care in using the technology given the rise of deepfakes. Fortune recalled that critics had accused the Olivers of politicising their son's death when they used AI to create a video of him in 2020, one YouTube commenter writing "They put words in a dead kid's mouth." (Fortune, 14 February 2024), to which the Olivers replied that their son's writings showed what he thought. No withdrawal or platform action was found.
Policy or guideline consequence: none found (no legislative effect was reported in the sources opened)
Academic discussion: none found in the sources opened (academic databases not yet searched for this case); Northeastern Global News (Cesareo Contreras, 22 March 2024) reports the views of two Northeastern University academics.

Case name: AI-enhanced bystander video of a triple fatal shooting, excluded as defence evidence in State of Washington v. Puloka (King County Superior Court)
Producer: The defence of Joshua Puloka, through a videographer and filmmaker it hired (not named in the sources opened), who had no forensic training and processed the bystander video with Topaz Labs software and Adobe Premiere Pro
Producer type: other (expert witness retained by defence counsel)
Country or context of the suffering depi: United States (Washington state: a shooting outside a bar in the Seattle area on 26 September 2021 in which three people were killed and two wounded)
Tool or model: Topaz Labs Video AI, followed by Adobe Premiere Pro (named in the court proceedings as reported by NBC News, ABA Litigation News and Criminal Legal News)
What the image depicts: A bystander's mobile phone recording of about ten seconds showing the confrontation and gunfire outside a bar, in which three people were killed, upscaled by machine learning so that the people involved are rendered with pixels predicted by the model rather than recorded by the camera.
Disclosure: statement: the defence put the exhibit before the court openly as an AI-enhanced version of the original recording, which the court admitted in its unaltered form (ABA Litigation News, Fall 2024; Greenberg Traurig, May 2024); no further wording was found in the sources opened.
Justification given by the producer: The defence filing described the enhanced version as a "faithful depiction of the original" (defence filing, quoted by NBC News, April 2024) and presented the enhancement as a way to make a low-resolution, blurry recording clearer for the jury in support of a self-defence claim [other (clarity of a low-resolution recording for a self-defence argument)]
Reception and debate: Prosecutors argued that the enhanced images could not be relied on and would mislead the jury, and their forensic video analyst, Grant Fredericks, testified that the software added visual information that was not in the original and lost some that was. Forensic video experts quoted by NBC News, including Jonathan Hak and George Reis, described the ruling as possibly the first of its kind in a United States criminal court and AI enhancement as premature for legal use, and Topaz Labs said it recommends against forensic or legal use of its product. The defence called the prosecution's criticisms exaggerated, and legal commentary since 2024 has treated the decision as the leading authority on AI-enhanced video evidence.
Policy or guideline consequence: Order of the King County Superior Court, signed on 29 March 2024, excluding the enhanced video under the Frye standard and Washington Evidence Rules 702, 401 and 403, on the ground that the output "does not show with integrity what actually happened" (the court's order as quoted by Criminal Legal News, December 2025); the trial proceeded on the unenhanced recording, the jury convicted in May 2024 and the defendant was sentenced on 21 June 2024 (Criminal Legal News). The ruling is cited in legal guidance for practitioners (ABA Litigation News, Fall 2024; Greenberg Traurig, May 2024).
Academic discussion: No academic article discussing the ruling was found; a search for legal scholarship returned practitioner commentary only (ABA Litigation News, Greenberg Traurig, Criminal Legal News). Case name: AI-enhanced stills of the killing of the Minneapolis intensive care nurse Alex Pretti by federal officers, shared as real frames of the video
Producer: Not identified: the image spread from a Facebook post of 25 January 2026 to Instagram, X and Threads (AFP); the AI Incident Database lists pro-Trump influencers, partisan online accounts and unidentified users among those who shared AI-altered images of the shooting
Producer type: other (anonymous and partisan social media accounts)
Country or context of the suffering depi: United States (Minneapolis, Minnesota: Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse and United States citizen, was shot dead by federal immigration officers on 24 January 2026)
Tool or model: not reported for the image examined by AFP; the AI Incident Database names Google's Gemini as the system allegedly used for altered images of the shooting
What the image depicts: AI-sharpened versions of frames from video of the killing, among them a still that shows officers around a kneeling man taken to be Pretti with a gun pointed at his head, in which the AI added details absent from the footage (an officer without a head, a leg bent at an unnatural angle next to an indiscernible object) while the item in his right hand, which authentic footage shows to be a phone, stayed blurred and was read by some viewers as a weapon, and images in which users ran AI enhancement over blurry footage to match a weapon photographed by the Department of Homeland Security (CP24).
Disclosure: none: the Facebook post that spread the image presented it as a still frame from the video, and the AI enhancement was identified only by fact-checkers (AFP Fact Check, 27 January 2026).
Justification given by the producer: none found
Reception and debate: AFP Fact Check rated the image manipulated after the GetReal Security laboratory co-founded by Hany Farid found it to be an AI enhancement of a real frame, and noted that the authentic video, verified by Bellingcat and The New York Times, shows Pretti holding a phone. Users read the image in opposite ways, some as proof of excessive force by the officers and others as proof that Pretti reached for a weapon, while CP24 reported that other users ran AI enhancement over blurry footage to match a weapon photographed by the Department of Homeland Security, producing a weapon that did not match. Giancarlo Fiorella of Bellingcat told CP24 that the tools cannot know what a person actually looks like and that labelling depends on the platforms, whose enforcement varies; the sources opened report no platform action against the image.
Policy or guideline consequence: none found (recorded as incident 1358 in the AI Incident Database, which classes it as disinformation that distorted evidence of the shooting)

Notes for the paper: The case is the counterpart of the Puloka ruling: the kind of AI sharpening that a court excluded as evidence circulated on platforms as a still frame of a killing, where it was read both as proof of police violence and as proof of a threat by the victim, so that the distinction of evidentiary versus appellative use does not hold once the image circulates in public. It raises the question of harm that survives disclosure, because the blurred object in the dead man's hand, which some viewers read as a weapon, supports an accusation against him that a later fact-check may not correct for those who saw the image. It also illustrates the regime that Chouliaraki, Stupart and Aiello call synthetic posthumanitarianism, in which the authenticity of an image of suffering is negotiated by fact-checkers, open-source investigators and platform labels after the image has circulated. The case groups the AI-enhanced still documented by AFP Fact Check and the AI-enhanced weapon images reported by CP24, both circulated as real frames of the same shooting; the AI Incident Database records AI-altered images of the shooting on the basis of a report by The New York Times.
